title: I Approved an AI-Written Database Migration in 90 Seconds. It Dropped a Production Table Live.
partialText:
The script looked clean. The commit message was better than most humans write. I still should have read it line by line, and I didn’t find out why until the table was already gone.

The pull request came in at 4:40 PM on a Thursday, an hour before I usually start winding down for the day. A schema migration, adding a new column to support a feature we’d been planning for weeks. The engineer who opened it had used an AI assistant to generate it, said so upfront in the description, which I appreciated. Transparent. Nothing to hide.

I skimmed it. Clean SQL, a sensible column type, a default value that made sense, a rollback script included, which most human-written migrations around here forget half the time. I approved it in about ninety seconds, the way you approve something that looks exactly like a hundred other migrations you’ve seen before.

It ran in staging fine. It ran in production twenty minutes later. And within about four minutes, a table that a completely unrelated service depended on was gone.

The Part I Skimmed Past

The migration had two statements in it. The first added the column, exactly as described. The second, a cleanup statement, was supposed to drop a temporary staging table that an earlier, unrelated migration had left behind months ago, clutter nobody had gotten around to removing.

Except the AI had gotten the table name subtly wrong. Not obviously wrong, not a typo you’d catch skimming. It had dropped a table with a nearly identical name to the actual temporary table, one character different, a table that a completely different service, one the engineer who wrote the migration didn’t even know existed, was actively reading from in production.

I found this out because that service started throwing errors within minutes, and someone on that team, who had no idea a migration had just run anywhere near their part of the system, started paging people trying to figure out why their database queries were suddenly failing against a table that no longer existed.

What I Actually Missed

Here’s the thing that still bothers me about this. I read the migration. I understood every line of SQL in it. Nothing about it was technically wrong in isolation. The syntax was correct, the logic was correct, the table name was a real table that existed in our database.

What I didn’t do was ask the question that would have actually caught it: what else in this system references a table with a name close enough to be confused with this one, and does the person who wrote this migration know that context exists. I was reviewing the SQL for correctness. I wasn’t reviewing it for the blast radius of a system I understood and the AI, and the engineer using it, didn’t.

That’s the actual gap. Not a knowledge gap. A context gap, and it’s specifically the kind of gap that AI-generated code is worst at revealing, because it writes with exactly the same confidence whether it understands your system’s full topology or none of it at all.

The Twenty Minutes That Actually Mattered

We didn’t lose data permanently, which I want to say plainly because it matters for how this story actually ends. The table had a recent backup, the outage was contained to about twenty minutes once we understood what had happened, and the fix itself, once we knew what was wrong, took about four minutes to apply.

The twenty minutes weren’t spent restoring a table. They were spent figuring out that a table had been dropped at all, because the error messages on the affected service’s side gave no indication that a migration on a completely different team’s schema was the cause. Two teams, two on-call engineers, working two ends of a problem that had one root cause neither of them could see from where they were standing.

The engineer who’d opened the original PR was mortified, understandably, and kept apologizing in the incident channel like this was some personal failure of judgment on his part. It wasn’t, not really. He’d used a tool the way the tool is designed to be used, gotten a plausible answer, and the plausible answer had a subtle, table-name-adjacent bug that neither he nor I caught because neither of us had the full picture of what else touched that part of the schema.

Why I Stopped Approving Migrations the Way I Used To

I changed exactly one thing about how I review database migrations after this, and it’s a question, not a checklist. Before approving anything that touches an existing table, drop, rename, alter, I now explicitly ask: what else in this system, that I might not immediately think of, could reference this exact name. Not “does this SQL look correct.” Whether anything downstream, anything I’m not already thinking about because it’s not the team that opened this PR, has a stake in the thing about to change.

It’s a slower question than skimming for syntax correctness. It’s also the only question that would have actually caught this specific failure, because the SQL itself was never wrong. The blast radius was invisible from inside the diff, and it was invisible specifically because AI-generated code doesn’t flag uncertainty about context it doesn’t have. A human writing this same migration, unfamiliar with that other service, might have left a comment asking someone to double check. The AI just wrote confident, syntactically perfect SQL that happened to be aimed at the wrong table by one character.

What This Actually Taught Me About Reviewing AI-Assisted Work

I don’t think the lesson here is to distrust AI-generated migrations more than human-written ones. Humans have dropped the wrong table before, plenty of times, long before any of this tooling existed. The lesson is narrower and, I think, more useful: the confidence of the output tells you nothing about how much of the actual system the output accounts for, and reviewing for correctness alone was never going to catch a mistake that was correct within its own limited view and wrong about everything outside it.

Now, on anything that touches shared infrastructure, a schema, a shared config, a queue another team reads from, I ask that context question explicitly, out loud, before I approve, human-written or AI-generated. It’s added maybe two minutes to a normal review. It’s the two minutes that would have saved us twenty, and would have saved another team’s on-call engineer an afternoon of confusion about why their database had apparently developed a mind of its own.

Where I Put the Rest

Understanding what actually makes an engineer trustworthy to approve changes like this, the systems-level judgment that catches what a clean diff can’t show you, and how to build that judgment deliberately instead of learning it the expensive way I did, is the whole reason I put together everything I’ve learned into one place: The Senior Backend Engineer Operating System: From the 3 AM Page to the Senior Offer.

If you’re reviewing AI-assisted changes on your own team right now and wondering what you might be skimming past, this is the map to the questions that actually catch it.

title: Google has already changed the job of writing code
partialText:
Nearly half of Google’s new code is generated by AI. The interesting part is what engineers are still responsible for.

The number that made me stop was not the claim that artificial intelligence can write code. We crossed that line a while ago. It was Google’s own description of its engineering work: nearly half of new code is generated by AI, then reviewed and accepted by engineers.

That sentence gets repeated as a jobs statistic. It is more useful as a description of a changing workday.

If a large engineering organization can move that much of its new code through an AI-assisted path, the job does not become “tell a machine what to build, then go home.” It becomes much more demanding in a less visible way. Someone still has to decide what should exist, whether the change fits the system, where it can fail, and whether a neat-looking patch has quietly made the next incident harder to understand.

I have seen the small version of this in ordinary software work. An assistant can produce a credible migration, test fixture, or API wrapper before I have finished making coffee. The dangerous moment comes after that. The diff is there. It compiles. It looks busy and competent. You still need enough context to notice that it created a timezone bug, widened a permission boundary, or copied a pattern that the rest of the codebase has spent two years trying to remove.

Google’s figure matters because it suggests that this is no longer a side experiment inside a few developer laptops. AI has entered the normal path by which code gets proposed, reviewed, and shipped. But the percentage is easy to misunderstand.

A generated line is not a completed decision

“Nearly half” sounds like AI now does half of an engineer’s job. It does not. A percentage of generated code tells us something about authorship at the keyboard. It says much less about who supplied the constraints, designed the interfaces, evaluated the risk, read the production signals, or carried the responsibility when the change went wrong.

Code generation works best where the problem has already been made legible. Give a model a clear function boundary, a mature test suite, familiar libraries, and a narrow task, and it can remove a lot of mechanical work. That is valuable. Nobody became a software engineer because they dreamed of writing the forty-seventh variation of a serializer or a database fixture.

The harder work begins when the specification is incomplete, buried in old decisions, or contradicted by what customers actually do. A model can make a plausible guess. Plausibility is not the same thing as correctness, and correctness is not the same thing as a safe change in a production system.

This is why “reviewed and accepted” is the most important part of Google’s statement. The review is not ceremonial. At scale, it is where an organization converts fast output into something it can defend later.

The bottleneck is moving upstream

For years, teams treated typing speed as a rough proxy for engineering output. It was never a great measure, but it was easy to see. AI makes the weakness obvious. If code arrives cheaply, then writing it cannot be the scarce resource anymore.

The scarce resource is clear judgment before generation and disciplined review after it. Good engineers will spend more time turning a fuzzy request into useful constraints: what must remain true, which systems are affected, which failure mode is unacceptable, and what evidence would make the change safe to release.

That changes how I think about prompts in coding tools. The best prompt is rarely a clever paragraph. It is often the context you have already built into the project: readable modules, useful tests, explicit ownership, logs that explain failures, and pull requests small enough for another human to reason about. A model benefits from all of that. So does the engineer reviewing it.

Teams that let AI spray changes across a poorly understood codebase may feel faster for a few weeks. Then the review queue becomes the new bottleneck, and the cost arrives as strange regressions, larger diffs, and a growing reluctance to touch parts of the system that nobody can fully explain.

The junior engineer question is real, but it is the wrong first question

People understandably jump from a number like Google’s to junior jobs. If AI writes the starter code, how does a new developer learn? That concern is legitimate. Early-career work has always included boring tasks that teach structure, debugging habits, and the feeling of a system resisting a bad assumption.

But protecting every repetitive task is not a serious training plan. The better question is whether teams are willing to teach judgment directly. Can a junior engineer explain why a generated change is safe? Can they trace a request through a service, write a failing test for an edge case, and say what metric would warn them if the release misbehaves?

Those are learnable skills, but they require deliberate feedback. A team cannot hand someone an AI assistant, accept the output, and assume that understanding will appear in the background.

Senior engineers have a version of the same problem. Their leverage may increase, but only if they stay close enough to the system to challenge confident output. Delegating the first draft is sensible. Delegating the mental model is how people end up approving code they cannot repair at 2 a.m.

What I would measure instead of generated-code percentage

Generated-code share is a good headline number. It is not a complete engineering metric. I would rather know whether AI-assisted changes have a different rollback rate, whether review time is rising or falling, and whether teams can still explain a service’s behavior when an incident begins.

I would also want to know where the tools are used. There is a large difference between generating internal test helpers and changing authorization logic. One speeds up a low-risk chore. The other may create a quiet security problem with a very polished diff attached to it.

This is not an argument for avoiding AI coding tools. I use them because they are useful, especially when the work is bounded and the feedback loop is tight. It is an argument against treating volume as the outcome. More generated code can mean less time spent typing. It can also mean more code that somebody must understand, own, and maintain.

The new job is to know when the machine is wrong

Google’s number points to a future that is already arriving in ordinary development teams. The keyboard is becoming less important than the decisions around it. That should be liberating for engineers who have been buried in repetitive work. It should also make us slightly uncomfortable.

When a model can produce a convincing implementation in seconds, confidence becomes cheap. Context, taste, and accountability do not. The engineer who can say “this is the wrong change, even though it looks right” may become more valuable, not less.

That is the part I keep coming back to. AI may write an increasing share of the code. Someone still has to be able to live with it after it ships.
